utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Gotovina, et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Two small procedural matters. Mr. Kehoe, during your cross-examination on Friday, you wondered what to do with a number of documents. I suggested that you would try to agree on a joint filing and bar table the documents involved. The Chamber was informed an agreement has been reached and that we could expect a joint filing bar tabling these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then there's another matter which is the Markac Defence was given until close of business today to come with some scheduling information. To the extent it would be possible already to give it around the first break that would be appreciated, because the Chamber has scheduled an internal meeting during the day and if we would not have that information, that would certainly -- well, not be a problem, but with your information it would be easier to have that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We will do so on the beginning of the next session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, Mr. Moric, I would like to remind you -- first of all, good morning to you as well. I would like to remind that you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony last week. Then, Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready to cross-examined Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I am thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, with leave of Court --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my apologies. Good morning to you and everyone in the courtroom. Before we start, may I ask your assistance on two points. I am not sure if I am familiar enough with the procedure. During the examination of Mrs. Prosecutor, may I indicate the documents that I know or I presume were earlier on admitted into evidence and be shown them so that I may answer the questions more easily?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If would you like to refer to documents which you have not available to yourself, please indicate so, and depending on what they are, and depending on what the question is, we'll then consider whether or not you can consult them. Yes. Any other matter, Mr. Moric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The other matter is this. During my examination of last week, I noticed that both parties made notes on paper. And I believe that I am somewhat handicapped in that regard. May I be given a pencil and a piece the paper so that I can make a note for myself. I would not be taking it out of the courtroom, nor would I be bringing into the courtroom any papers from the outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the first is of less concern to us than the second would be. If you would like to make notes when a question is asked, then there should be no problem. But, if you have any written documents, whether personal notes or anything else you brought with you, and if you would like to consult it, you should first seek permission to do so. But I see you're nodding, no, that you didn't bring anything. Then matters are clear. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With leave of Court if I could also have the transcript -- hard copy of the transcript given to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And could someone provide Mr. Moric with a clean piece of paper, or even a few, and a pen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In preparation for your testimony here, did you have the opportunity to meet any of the Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before entering the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Before entering the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was preparing with the Defence team that called me as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How many times did you meet with -- your -- I presume when you said "the Defence team," you're referring to the Defence team for Mr. Markac; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, of course. I am the witness for the Defence of General Markac.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you meet any of the other two Defence teams, either the Defence team for Mr. Gotovina or the Defence team for Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I met with them briefly too.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court how many times you met each of the teams in preparation for testimony; that is, the Markac team, the Gotovina Defence team, and the Defence team for Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met with each of the three Defence teams once; and, of course, the meeting with the Defence for General Markac was much longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And in the course of those meetings, were you shown documents?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some of the documents, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you -- were those documents familiar to you? Were those documents issued by you, or were there also other documents that you had not seen prior to that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that there was discussion of documents I didn't see. We mostly discussed the documents that I saw and the documents that I wrote and signed at -- at a certain point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you informed or was there a discussion about the evidence that has been already led in these proceedings, evidence of other witnesses or documentary evidence? Was there a discussion with you about that evidence? By any one of the teams.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies, Mrs. Prosecutor, if I misunderstood your question. You're asking me if the Defence teams discussed statements of other witnesses who have so far testified before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't discuss that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, your testimony is that you were in charge of Operation Povratak or Operation Return, as it is known. Now, as a person in charge of OA Povratak when reports were sent to the Ministry of Interior addressed to the OA Povratak staff, did those reports reach you or were you informed of the contents of those reports by any person?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, reports reached me. Some of the reports did not reach me, but it depended on their substance and on my whereabouts at the time, whether I was in the office or away. In that case the report would have reached the chief of the sector or, as I've already called him, to make it more easily understandable, to the head of the personnel of the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And in those instances, when reports did not reach you because you were not present in the ministry premises, were you, afterwards, informed of the contents of the reports by the -- the chief of the sector?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the contents, relevance, or less of the report. But, in principle, he should have informed me thereof.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during examination of Mr. Kay, he discussed with you a whole series of documents relating to the operation, security operation known as OA Knin 95. And that was a highly organised, coordinated security operation providing security for the liberty train, isn't that correct, which reached Knin on 26th August?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, that -- in -- in organising that operation, the forces of the Ministry of Interior coordinated and worked in cooperation with the military police; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Prosecutor, among others, the military police was involved too. In that particular operation, absolutely all security services of the Republic of Croatia were involved, including, of course, the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And about how many members of the Ministry of Interior were used for that operation? I'm talking about fundamental police firstly.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to specify. I can only speculate, based on --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you give an approximate figure, sort of ballpark figure. You don't have to be very specific on the exact figures.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I think back about the railway line, which the freedom train took, and the regular police obligations attached to high-risk travels, then I can think of the enormous duties in the places where the train stopped; whereas, for the police the duties were mostly attached to the line where the train ran. It could have involved in terms of any direct participation, some 300 to 400 policemen. As soon as the train left the section of the area they covered, they would be relieved of some of the duties that they had previously.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And are you able to give some idea as to about how many members of the military police were used for the operation? If you don't know, you could say you don't know; if you can give us perhaps a ballpark figure, then please do so.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this high-risk security operation, it was not realistic to expect any high-risk security for the military police force. I cannot, unfortunately, assess what the strength of the military police involved was. What I can state with certainty is that the numbers were far lower than the number of the civilian policeman involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And for how long did the preparations go on, until the 26th?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were able to see from the document, the preparations were conducted by the national security office. I can't gauge how long their preparations took, but if you're asking me how long it took the civilian police to get involved in the action, I could tell you a few things about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, I don't mean to be rude. I'm asking for what you know, so if you could just let us know, based on your understanding, the preparation for civilian police, how long it took. And if you could try to be brief in your responses, I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will be brief, Mrs. Prosecutor. I don't know how long the preparations took from the viewpoint of national security, but the preparations of the civilian police did not take long, because the police was always present in its area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So are you able to give us any idea. Is it not very long, is it a week, a few days? If you could just give us some idea.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two days.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did you have any problems about coordination between the military police during this particular operation?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that we had any problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now is it also correct that in the run-up to the -- the arrival of the liberty train there were a series of mop-up operations carried out in the area by the special police to provide further security for the train, from 21st August downwards?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but probably under the term "mop-up" you mean the police searches of a terrain?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's what -- if I ever I use the word "mop-up" I refer to the terrain clearance operations.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apologise my digression, but the "mop-up" term is not a police term. That's why I wanted to be quite sure of what it is that you meant. It wasn't just in -- prior to this particular action, but the searches had to be carried out in general, and, of course, then also in preparation for the journey that the President of the Republic and the government members would take.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, as a member of the committee, if there were any breaches of security in the area, particularly close to the area where the train was travelling through, would you have been informed of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, I would have had to have been informed, save if the piece of information fell under the remit of national security and were classified as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, were you informed that there were -- there was some combat activity in an area - and I will be very specific - in an area called Ramljane, which is not too distant from the rail track on 26th August. That's the day that the train was scheduled to arrive in Knin. Were you informed that?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since that was a period of time that was quite eventful, I'm not sure if I was, indeed, informed of it. But I believe that I would be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I didn't ask you whether you would be, Mr. Moric. My question was: To your recollection, were you informed that there was combat activity in an area called Ramljane, which is not too distant from the rail track on the very day the President was arriving in Knin. Do you remember that, or don't you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Madam Prosecutor. Unfortunately, the only correct answer is that I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, were you present in Knin on 25th and 26th August because of the arrival of the liberty train in Knin on 26th? And I'm referring to both days: 25th and 26th, or 25th or 26th.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, it -- that was not the reason. I was not in Knin because of the arrival of the train. I was there because of the general context, and I believe that I was also there on the 25th and the 26th. I'm sure that I was there on the day when the President of the state arrived in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Moric, I'm it going to discuss with you a particular topic about which much evidence has been led in these proceedings, and you yourself have discussed this at length with the investigators of the OTP, and that's about events in Grubori. Now when did you learn for the first time of -- that an incident had occurred in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. I don't remember when it was that I learned for the first time. But I remember that it was a few days, a couple of days or even a few more days after the event.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Who informed you of -- of the event?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't remember that either. A lot of information reached us from all over the place at the time. It could have been one of my staff who acted as the coordinator in the area. I'm not sure whether it was perhaps Mr. Tomurad or Mr. Franjo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, were you informed that the incident related to the -- the -- the death, killings of five civilians and burning of several houses?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Madam Prosecutor. That's not how I was informed. I did not receive any particular data. All I learnt was that there had been an event, not an incident, but, rather, an event, with some casualties. The information was not specific at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So can you tell us what was conveyed to you? You say "not an incident, an event." But could you tell the Trial Chamber what really was conveyed to you in that first information. Were you told that civilians had died in the event?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that the information I was conveyed spoke about an event, which involved casualties. No numbers were mentioned, and the event was not qualified in any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And were you told that the casualties were civilians?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I understood the information. The way I understood it was that the victims in question were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge, was this event investigated by any sector of the Ministry of Interior? And I don't want you to speculate, Mr. Moric. I just want you to tell the Trial Chamber what you know.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for a fact, Madam Prosecutor, because I wanted to make sure, I wanted to check that the event was recorded at the Knin police station, and that the information about the event was conveyed was to the chief of the police administration and the head of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, your testimony was that, in fact this is at transcript reference T-25634 and 635, you testified here that information generally was passed on from the police station to the police administration, and from the police administration it went on to the Ministry of Interior. Now, to your knowledge did your report -- now in fact the Trial Chamber is in receipt of the Knin police station log which records the event and the Knin -- Zadar-Knin police administration log which, too, records the event. Now, to your knowledge, was a report sent from the Zadar-Knin police administration to the Ministry of Interior about the event in Grubori, as it was recorded by them?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that report. However, as per rules, it should have reached the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, during the examinations of, I believe, when Mr. Kay examined you, we see a series of reports from the police administration chiefs to you, which records on-site investigations in relation to arson and theft. Now, you said after a few days from this incident you learnt that an event had occurred and there were casualties, civilian casualties. Wouldn't you have expected to then also receive a report from the Zadar-Knin police administration chief on the on-site investigation into the deaths of those civilians? Weren't you expecting to receive that report?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Madam Prosecutor, I did not expect that, and I should not have expected that. Such a report along the professional lines goes to the crime police sector of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, your testimony here is, and I can cite exactly what you said, that -- that it was a duty of the fundamental police to secure the crime site and secure the evidence until the crime police arrives. And we saw in fact your report sent by the chiefs of police administration giving you numbers of on-site investigation into arson and theft. So why wouldn't you expect to receive a report on an on-site investigation, how they secured the site? On this event, killing -- killings, why is it that when it comes to this particular event, you don't expect a report on the on-site investigation from the fundamental police?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, in the report that you have just quoted, you will not find information about the events which were potentially attacks against human lives, because those would be grave crimes or potentially grave crimes. In other words, it was the crime police that should have been informed about that and should have primarily dealt with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand your testimony, Mr. Moric. Is it your position, then, that when it comes to on-site investigations into killings, the fundamental police -- members of the fundamental police don't participate in the on-site investigation at all? Is that -- is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. Of course, they do. However, as you may have noticed in the documents that we discussed last week, fortunately enough we had in the area a substantially low number of aggravated crimes and killings. By contrast, we had a lot of attacks against abandoned property, and we -- we dealt with larger numbers. Obviously not ignoring the other incidents. However, when it comes to murder attempts, the fundamental police is -- are involved, but the crime police is professionally involved and deals with it along professional lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, I understand that, Mr. Moric. But isn't it the case that in the -- when it comes to arson and theft, it's the fundamental police that initially secures the crime site and the evidence, and thereafter the crime police conducts the investigation, when it comes to arson and theft. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And while the on-site investigation is going on, for as long as it lasts, the fundamental police do have things to do one site, while the crime police are doing their job.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, it is on the basis of that involvement in the on-site investigations of the fundamental police that you received the reports on arson and theft that we saw during your examination. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those reports are sent by the chiefs of police administrations as we have seen. They report on the trends and on the problems segregated by types.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now in the same vein, in cases of killings, the crime site is secured by the fundamental police and until the crime investigation police -- crime takes over. They secure the site, they secure the evidence, and participate in the same way they would participate in the case of an arson. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Madam Prosecutor. But a small correction. Not until the crime police takes over, but all the time, for as long as the crime police are involved, and also depending on what the crime police expect from the fundamental police. During the entire onsite investigation, unfortunately, the fundamental police have things to do and are involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So why wouldn't the fundamental police then not send you a report on on-site investigations conducted into killing incidents? What is the difference? I fail to see the difference, Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it seems, it seems that you really fail to see the difference, and I may be of assistance. The difference lies in the gravity of the problem. If an event involves the death of one or more people, then potentially we are dealing with an aggravated crime, with a grave crime which specifically engages and involves both types of police but primarily the crime police. And one shouldn't assume that the crime police, along the lines of their organisation and responsibility, will not inform all those who should be informed, including the Ministry of Interior. We have discussed the documents, we discussed the documents last week, and you could see from those documents that we dealt with the prevention of those crimes, which actually represented a large number of incidents. Fortunately enough, those did not involve a high number of grave crimes, including the attacks on civilians. In that huge number, we had a prevailing number of other problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Moric, let me move on without wasting any more time on that issue. Would you be surprised to be told that this Trial Chamber has heard evidence that no sector of the Ministry of Interior conducted an investigation into what happened in Grubori until 2001, when the State Prosecutor, Mr. Zganjer, initiated an investigation? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I know of that only partially. I'm not surprised to hear that fact. In practice, in the practice of almost all police forces worldwide, there are the so-called cases, cold cases, which need to be investigated, even ten years after the event.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, that wasn't my question. My question is: Are you aware that the incident has not been investigated by any sector of the Ministry of Interior until 2001? The event happened in 1995. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I don't know why you are insisting on saying not a single sector since -- you know that there is only one sector in the Ministry of the Interior which deals with such crimes, and that is the sector of crime police. As far as I know, from the time when I was affiliated with the Ministry of Interior, the problem lay in the fact that it had never been established what had happened there, whether a crime did happen or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question is, Mr. Moric, did you know that the crime police -- if that's what you want to say, you say there is only one sector which they investigated, let me ask you: Did you know that the crime police never investigated what happened in Grubori, even to establish as to what had happened, never conducted any investigations into the incident until 2001? This Trial Chamber has heard that evidence. Did you know that as an assistant minister?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in such a way. And that was not my responsibility. I was not duty-bound to learn something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, your subordinate officer Mr. Cetina, chief of Zadar-Knin police administration testified here. He was aware of that fact. And this is transcript reference 23518 to 23519, and he did in fact acknowledge that the police had not investigated the events in Grubori. Now, there's also evidence that has been led in this Court, and I refer to P35, where UN Human Rights Action Team visiting the crime site over two weeks after the incident found bullet casings still uncollected by the police at the crime site. Now, you have testified here that it was the duty of the fundamental police to secure a site and collect the evidence, which shows that, actually, even the fundamental police in this instance hasn't done anything with regard to investigations. What do you have to say about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, in your questions to the former assistant minister for the fundamental police you are trying to equate him as a member of the fundamental police involved in investigation. The members of the fundamental police are trained and equipped to go to a site and to be able to recognise what that site represents. They know how to secure that area, and they now how to recognise the potential of possible evidence about the event. They also know how to recognise who the potential witnesses are. This is more or less what the fundamental police is supposed to on-site. On the other hand, if Mr. Cetina, in his testimony, said what you have just quoted back to me - and there's no reason for me to doubt your words - then in accordance with the provisions of the Law on Internal Affairs, Mr. Cetina was talking about the responsibility of the police administration and a police station. The law clearly prescribes that, at that time, a police station was in charge of monitoring the situation and the events in its area and undertook measures to implement the law. Furthermore, the law charges a police station and a police administration for the area for which it was established, and finally the ministry with responsibility for the entire state. Madam Prosecutor, subsidiary responsibility is prescribed in performing legally prescribed duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, you're the assistant minister in charge of fundamental police, you were in 1991, and the more senior member of the Ministry of Interior who has testified in these proceedings up to date. Now, I have placed before you the fact that the fundamental police did not carry out an on-site investigation into an incident of killing of civilians and burning of houses which you were made aware of a few days after the incident, and your response is to me is that I'm equating you to a member of the fundamental police, which I'm trying to do. I'm just asking you if you're in a position to offer an explanation to the Trial Chamber as to why the fundamental police, your subordinates, failed to carry out a -- an on-site investigation into this serious crime. Are you able to offer an explanation to the Trial Chamber, as the person in charge of the financial police?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, Madam Prosecutor, I can, as I have so far. The fundamental police are not in charge of carrying out an on-site investigation. They do not carry out criminal proceedings. They just secure the site. If the fundamental police have not performed their task in keeping with the law, or as provided for by the law -- I have described for you the levels of subsidiary responsibility that existed at the time. Madam Prosecutor, at that time, there were a total of 11.000 police officers in the Republic of Croatia, and every day, one of them failed to do something or omitted to do something, but there were levels above him to punish that or sanction that. But it wasn't me. At that time I could not know, nor was it expect from me, nor was the ministry organised in such a way that would enable me to learn about every concrete case and to be able to know whether the fundamental police had done everything they were supposed to do or if, by contrast, a police officer made a mistake or failed to do his duty properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. In the interests of time, Mr. Moric, let me just move on. Isn't it correct, and you -- I believe you're fully of this fact because you have spoken about this matter. Isn't it correct that the police coordinator, Mr. Buhin, in fact wanted to have this event investigated, but Mr. Sacic from the special police arrived in Knin and tried to delay the investigations or prevent the investigations. And the result of that situation was that you withdrew Mr. Buhin from Knin to Zagreb. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, unfortunately, you're not right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you explain why I'm not right, Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must, and I will. According to information I received about the event, a few days after event, in the police circles, including Mr. Buhin and Mr. Sacic, whom you have mentioned, there were controversial opinions or, rather, a conflict between professional opinions as to what had actually happened there. There was an opinion, according to which the victims were a consequence of a crime, and there was also an opinion that they were not, but, rather, that there were collateral damage in a conflict between the special police and the remains of paramilitary or a para-police or some other type of armed conflict. According to information that I had at the time, Mr. Sacic was angry, as a matter of fact, and he had every right to be angry, that the problem had not been solved and resolved and that there were still doubts as to what had happened. And as for Mr. Buhin, it is true I withdrew him to Zagreb, but I -- I did that because it was time for his rotation, for him to be replaced, just like with any other coordinator. That was one reason. And the second reason was the fact that in that concrete case, he did not give initiative to his colleagues from the crime police, and he did not help them in doing their job to the extent a person from the fundamental police could. It was not for any other reason that he was withdrawn to Zagreb, as you suggested.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric let me take to your statement given to the -- the OTP, the interview. And if could I ask you to turn to the third section. That is 48 -- V000-4894 that's a final section, Mr. Moric. And if could you turn to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's D1842, on e-court page 224, or it could also be traced through 4894, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Have you found -- it's page 3, Mr. Moric. It's the last section. Under the last tab.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] This one?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Page 3.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You were asked about this event, and this is your response. You say: "Yes, I know why he was -- why he returned to Zagreb. He was in conflict in a professional sense with the special police because they were crossed. They were mad, that this case didn't go into our crime, that the crime police did not deal with this case immediately, but it was waited for a day or two until somebody from Zagreb came. I think it was Mr. Sacic who came from Zagreb, and then it was dealt with. And I felt that it was not good to leave him in a situation where there is so much tension, regarding the time-period. So, I called him back to Zagreb." "And in my assessment there was a combination of two reasons why this conflict occurred."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Going to the next page, page 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You say: "One of the reasons why they did not agree on the ... on the story how this event came about. "And then the second conflict was in continuation of that, ... they did not agree what actually happened was that when the procedure was supposed to ... whether or not there should be a procedure, and if there should be a procedure, should it be immediate. "And that [sic] was clear to me that these ... that this event was ... was recorded, and there is no way now to stop the normal police procedure." And then you go on: "Then I thought that it would be better for Mr. Buhin to go back to Zagreb and not leave them -- not leave him in that conflict situation." Then Mr. Foster puts an question to you: "Right. I'm trying to understand that because it seems to the reverse of what I was told. It was Mr. Buhin and the chief of police administration, Mr. Romanic, who wanted to investigate it straight away. And it was Mr. Sacic who did not wanted that to happen." If could you go to page 5, you respond: "Yes, you're right. Allegedly, that was the reason that they were in conflict. Maybe I interpreted ... maybe I related the thing wrongly, but [sic] ... yes, that was the essence of their conflict." Then you clarify Mr. Moric: "What I know for sure is that the reason for conflict was that one side wanted investigation immediately and the other side wanted investigation little bit later on. Which side wanted which, I'm not so ... I'm not so positive on, but it's that what's the reason of a conflict. But I believe that Buhin and Romanic" -- this is at page 6 "as a professional policemen with many years of experience wanted to deal with things according to regular police procedure, which is to deal with [sic] immediately. But knowing Buhin and my ... associates, nobody could have influenced them that things are done in any way other than the way they should have been done." Then you are asked the question: "Why did ... Mr. Sacic of the special police not [sic] want to go according to proper procedure?" And you respond, that's page 7: "Probably he wanted to see for himself what happened. I don't see" -- then there is further ... further conversation about that. "I don't see how that would stop normal procedure continuing." And you respond, "yes, I agree, but you ask me what do I think, why did he do it, and I'm just assuming. If I were him, I wouldn't even go there." And you finally -- then you are asked a question: "I suppose it highlights one of the difficulties that your men working under during that period of time?" And at page 8, you respond: "Yes, that's why I chose people to send there according to special criteria. I wanted experienced policemen with very stable personalities." Now, I'm trying -- now, this is what you have testified, this is in evidence, Mr. Moric. If I could understand your testimony here, Mr. Buhin wanted to investigation the crime, and Mr. Sacic wanted to delay the investigations. That's how you understood the matters. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mrs. Prosecutor. As I was following what you were indicating in the transcript, I observed you quoting that I agreed with what Mr. Foster said. And as you can see from the conversation, Mr. Foster suggested what my answer to the question would be. And I can see in my answer that I'm speculating. You can see at page 7, line 9, I'm telling him I agree, but you asked me what my assumption was, and I'm speculating, just as you are. That's in line 9. Since I was never sent this transcript and I have never had occasion to review it, I'm not sure that I was either translated or interpreted correctly in what I said here. But I will answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, if I could stop you there for a minute --

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My perception of the events at the time --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I could stop you there for a minute. I just want to let you know, if you wish to, we have the video recording here, and I have the exact timings of your answers. If you wish to, I can play it to you so that can you see for yourself what you are saying. I just wanted to let you know before. So please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not doubt that you can. But I what I wanted to say was that it would have been proper for the transcript to be sent to me earlier on. But if this isn't something that is required by the rules, let's forget it. The way I understood the matter at the time, Mr. Buhin was a professional policeman, absolutely so, and this was not called into question in this conversation either. Whatever the situation was, he demanded that the matter be approached professionally. What from I understood, Mr. Sacic was cross because the matter had not been resolved right away, either through an investigation by the crime police, or through a combination of the involvement of the crime police and the sanitization team which also comprised a crime-scene examiner. Why wasn't it decided right away whether this was a crime and then a criminal investigation would follow? Or why it wasn't decided -- of course, in the case it was decided that it was collateral damage, then the sanitization was to be commenced right away. In other words, he was cross because the decision was not made right away.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, I'm going to read again to you what you -- what is in evidence, what you said. This is what you say: "What I know for sure" -- this is at page 5 of D1842, the section V000-4894. This is what you say: "What I know for sure is that the reason for conflict was that one side wanted investigation immediately and the other side wanted investigation a little bit later on. Which side wanted which, I'm not so ... positive, but that's what the reason of a conflict." That's what you say. And if you want, we can play your answer back to you on audio. So what you're saying is, the conflict was because one side wanted the matter investigated immediately, the other side wanted the matter delayed. Now, you didn't know which side wanted which. But the result was that you withdrew Mr. Buhin to Zagreb. Now, isn't it correct if one of these parties wanted the matter delayed, then obviously that party is obstructing an investigation. It's not wanting matters to proceed according to law. Because an investigation should take -- be started immediately. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So now, your testimony here was that Mr. Buhin wanted. I read back exactly what you said: "The way I understand the matter at the time Mr. Buhin was a professional policeman [indiscernible], and this was not called into question in this conversation either. Whatever the situation was, he demanded that the matter be approached professionally." So if Mr. Buhin wanted the matter approached professionally, that would then indicate that he wanted the matter investigated immediately. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In which event the party that wanted the matter delayed would have to be Mr. Sacic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information I had, Mr. Sacic came upon this situation where there was a conflict of professional opinions as to what had exactly transpired. When he realised that there was a conflict of opinion, he was cross for the fact that a decision had not been made at once. And then, based on the decision, a procedure had not been initiated, either a criminal investigation into the perpetrators of the crime, or if it was collateral damage, then in, according with the Geneva Conventions identification of the victims and the preservation of traces that would indicate their identities, all in keeping with the Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric you're a senior police officer. It's not -- before talking about opinions as to what happened, don't you think what should be done is to investigate, carry out an investigation, and thereafter, based on the information decide as to what happened? How could you entertain Mr. Sacic's issue about opinions, conflict of opinions as to what happened? What should have been done is to conduct an investigation immediately; isn't that correct? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, you're right. I understand, and you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Then if you agree with me on that, if is there another party suggesting the matter should be delayed because there is some conflict of opinion as to what really happened, that is not relevant, isn't it? What you should be proposing and advocating is that the matter should be immediately investigated?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's what Mr. Buhin wanted, isn't it? Mr. Buhin wanted the matter investigated.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. And he should have asked for the head of the police station, he should have made sure that the head of the police station was informed, and that would have initiated the whole procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Why did you withdraw him to Zagreb? Here was your police coordinator who wants to have the matter investigated. There is another person, Mr. Sacic is bringing a completely relevant issue into that process. Why would you want to withdraw him to Zagreb at a particular time like that?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't withdraw him at that critical point. Rather, it was several days later. Mrs. Prosecutor, I said that time had come for Mr. Buhin to be replaced under the normal system of rotation. Evidently, the police station was informed, and the crime police of the police administration was informed, too, as was the police administration of Knin. In other words, conditions were met for the police to start proceeding, and that's the most relevant matter. Thereafter, the responsible persons at all levels were supposed to take measures in keeping with the law, regardless of whether Mr. Buhin was there or not. The fact that Mr. Buhin was there did not matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, I want to let you know that you're contradicting your own testimony here. Your testimony here, very clearly, and it's on record, is that you withdrew Mr. Buhin to Zagreb because of that conflict. In fact, you know, Mr. Foster has questioned you at depth about why you would want to withdraw him to Zagreb and how the conflict would affect the police activity, and you have clearly stated that the reason for withdrawal was the conflict. And now you're saying that the reason was because it was time for rotation, which is a complete contradiction. How do you reconcile your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Mrs. Prosecutor, you are right. A moment ago, I only mentioned rotation as the reason. However, previously in answer to your one of your questions, I cited both reasons as the reasons for his withdrawal. Namely, the rotation and the conflict of professional opinions. And that's the correct answer. As far as my conversation with Mr. Foster is concerned, you can see that he insisted on this matter alone. Of course, he wasn't interested in organisational and other aspects of work in the field, and that's why I did not discuss with him the rotation periods of the men dispatched to the field, including that of Mr. Buhin.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic [sic], you were asked as to why you withdrew Mr. Buhin, and you never ever informed Mr. Foster as to this new reason that you're giving today. You only discussed about the conflict. You said -- in fact, let me read again your -- you reiterated that again at page 34. If you could turn to page -- it starts at page 33. Mr. Foster again asked you this question: "Okay. Why remove Mr. Buhin? You say because of conflict with Sacic. Bearing" --

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is that I'm sorry, I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Page 33, if you turn on the same section.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Page 33.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, my -- oh, right, I'm sorry. I have found it. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is what you say. You are ask the question: "Okay why remove Mr. Buhin? You say because of conflict with Sacic. Bearing in mind that the special police were doing work elsewhere, how often were they likely to meet up?" Mr. Foster is asking you about the issue of conflict. And at page 34 you say this: "No, this is not a case only of personal conflict between them two. I thought about the possible implications of that conflict in between the two of them." Then you are asked: "Why leave Buhin in such an atmosphere where can he get into another conflict which would be even more and even more expressed because what happened before? I am certain that other people in special police knew about them ... knew about that conflict, not only Sacic." Mr. Moric, you have had ample opportunity to tell Mr. Foster if there was another reason for Mr. Buhin's withdrawal. You have in fact reiterated that it was a conflict that made you withdraw Mr. Buhin to Zagreb. And now you are coming out with this new position of rotation. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber - you are under oath - as to what the truth is.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Prosecutor, I could not have discussed organisational and other aspects of work with Mr. Foster, as can you well see from the transcript. He was solely focused on this, and it is only understandable. Let me repeat, that there were two reasons, namely rotation and conflict of professional opinions. And I'm telling you this under the solemn declaration that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Isn't it correct, Mr. Buhin [sic], that prior to withdrawing -- sorry, Mr. Sacic -- Moric, that prior to withdrawing Mr. Buhin to Zagreb, you telephoned him and told him angrily not to interfere into crime police work. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that I frequently communicated with my men who were in the area. There was several reasons for it. And, on occasion, it had to do with a specific task. So I don't rule out the possibility, and I probably did call Mr. Buhin and tell him, just as I did many times previously in our cooperation, that he should not encroach upon the competence of others; namely, the crime police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: But why were you angry, Mr. Moric? Mr. Buhin was just trying to have crime investigated. Why would you be angry about this? Because I can tell you -- I can read back the testimony of Mr. Buhin given in this Court. His testimony is that you telephoned and angrily told him not to interfere in the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could we first establish what the witness reasons about the time of that telephone conversation. You say you didn't exclude for the possibility that you may have called Mr. Buhin, did you mean to say that that was in relation to the Grubori incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember specifically, Your Honour, when it was that I phoned him, and I can therefore not rule out the possibility that it happened at the time when the Grubori incident was topical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you earlier testified that you couldn't deal with all incidents that happened, so many police people around. Now, here we find an incident for which, at least evidence was received by this Chamber, for which Mr. Sacic especially travels from Zagreb, which - but please correct me when I'm wrong - would not be the usual thing to do for whatever incident, would it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you're asking me about Mr. Sacic's trip?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether that was usual for every incident to travel a long distance in difficult times.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From my experience, I can tell you, Your Honour, that there were cases whose weight required a trip to be made. Now, whether that was a rule in the special police force as well, I can't tell you that, based on my experience. I think that the size of the problems we were faced with out in the field would warrant trips to be made, and I can tell you that that was true for my sector of the uniformed police, for the sector of the special police, and the crime police. Now, whether this was, from the perspective of the special police, something that warranted it ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Earlier you told us, more or less in between the lines, that so many things happened, that why would this incident or this event, why would you remember anything about it? Now, apparently, the matter was important enough for Mr. Sacic to travel a long distance from Zagreb, to Gracac and Knin. Which would make it at least not an average event or an average incident, would it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with that, Your Honour. You can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you aware that Mr. Sacic had travelled down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, Your Honour, I heard later that he had travelled there. I didn't know that he had been sent. Nobody informed me about that, because there was no reason to inform me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you mean to say, is it your testimony that when Mr. Sacic travelled down and when a dispute arose about whether or not to immediately investigate, that you were not aware that Mr. Sacic had travelled down and that this problem had arisen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is exactly what I wanted to say. I was informed about the event, and, later on, I learned that Mr. Sacic had been there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you been in touch with anyone who was there and involved in this dispute about whether or not to investigate at that very moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was not in contact with anybody. I don't remember having been in contact with anybody. Only later I was in contact with Mr. Buhin, but I don't remember anybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean by later, that you were in contact with Mr. Buhin? What is "later" in this respect? What day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I meant to say was that I am referring to the contact with Mr. Buhin about which Madam Prosecutor asked me. Two or three days after the event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember that I was in contact with Mr. Buhin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just a couple of minutes ago you said that you were not sure whether you had. It could well be that you would have had a telephone conversation, but you had no recollection about that. And then you were asked whether that was in relation to the Grubori incident. And you said, Well, maybe, I don't know. And now, apparently, you have some recollection. Could you give us the details of that telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that apparently is, Ms Mahindaratne, what you would like to hear from the witness; is that correct? So give us all details you remember from that telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember that I told him like a few times before, in similar situations, to hand the matter over to the crime police, let them do their part of the job. And I reminded him that he was supposed to return to Zagreb and to be replaced by other people in the -- who were coming to the area. If I remember properly, those were experts from the ministry dealing with traffic control and border control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, let me read one of your previous answers. I asked you: "You say you didn't exclude for the possibility that you may have called Mr. Buhin. Did you mean to say that that was in relation to the Grubori incident?" The answer was: "I can't remember specifically, Your Honour, when it was that I phoned him, and I can therefore not rule out the possibility that it happened at the time when the Grubori incident was topical." Now, from your last answers, I take it that it was specifically on the Grubori incident that you had a telephone conversation with him after two or three days. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as for the event in Grubori, I learnt about it two or three days after the event. And the conversation with Mr. Buhin may have taken place even one or two days later than that, but I can't be sure. So that conversation may have taken place maybe three to five days after the event, because, as far as I can remember, I learnt about the event a couple of days after it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If, therefore, Mr. Buhin says that it was on the 27th of August, you would say that that is not accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To my recollection, that conversation should have taken place later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you inform Mr. Buhin before that he had return to Zagreb, apparently in the context of rotation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, everybody was informed -- informed and Mr. Buhin was also informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you specifically talk with him about his return soon to Zagreb, in the context of rotation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Before they were centered there, the head of personnel spoke to everybody and announced that they would be rotated, depending on the scope of problems on the ground and the requirements for other types of experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And in that telephone conversations with Mr. Buhin, in relation to the Grubori incident, he was, for the first time, informed specifically that it was now his time to return to Zagreb. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I was the one who told him that for the first time. However, the head of personnel had announced that even before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As you said before, that rotation was depending on the scope of the problems on the ground and the requirement for other types of experts. Was there any schedule put on paper about rotation in advance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was the chief of sector who dealt with that, the head of personnel, that is. And rotation depended on the need for other types of experts and estimates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, my question was not whether you would repeat the criteria but whether it was put on paper. May I take it from your answer that you're not aware of any rotation scheme put on paper in which Mr. Buhin was expected to return to Zagreb at that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. If there was such a rotation scheme, it was the head of personnel who had it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What, then, were your specific concerns about rotation? Because you said it was two reasons, whereas, you say the rotation was in the hands of the head of personnel, whereas I understand you were involved in the conflicting views -- conflicting professional views. What was your knowledge, more precisely, on what rotation required at that very moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that at that time, people who had to be sent to the field were from the sector of traffic control and border control and some other types of experts and that I had been informed about that by the head personnel. And that was the main motive why Mr. Buhin had to be rotated, as well as the other coordinators after him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not only time for a break, but it is already far beyond the time for a break. Ms. Mahindaratne, the questions I put to the witness should not be understood in any way as that you -- that we would have explored sufficiently. I leave it entirely to you whether this still needs further attention or not. We will have a break, and we will resume at ten minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll deal with a few procedural matters at the end of this session, but since Mr. Moric is in the courtroom -- yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just -- I just want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I just want to inform the Chamber according to your request from the beginning of the session that I sent and an e-mail to Court Officer and to all parties of the case as it refers to our schedule for the rest of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a very practical way of resolving the matter. The other procedural matters, there are two small ones, wait with them until the end of this session so that Mr. Moric is not -- is not in a position that he has to listen to all kind of matters which are of no concern to him. At least they should not be of any concern to him. Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. May I just a clarification, Mr. President. At the break, did Your Honour say the questions I put to the witness should not be understood in any way that we have not explored sufficiently?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would not in any way limit you in exploring the matter, and the fact that I have put some questions in relation to this shouldn't cause to you refrain from any relevant an important matter would you still want to ask him about it or any further details.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, I just have a few questions on that subject we were discussing before I move on. Now, you were asked a question by the Bench, as to whether you specifically -- let me just -- you were asked: "And in the telephone conversation with Mr. Buhin in relation to the Grubori incident, he was, for the first time, informed specifically, that it was now his time to return to Zagreb." That is the question from the Bench. And your answer is: "I believe that I was the one who told him that for the first time. However, the head of personnel had announced that even before." Now, that wasn't quite exactly an answer to the question. The question was, did you inform Mr. Buhin that he had to return to Zagreb in the course of the telephone conversation when you discussed the conflict about the Grubori event, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I told him, but that doesn't mean that he had not been aware of that same announcement from before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Moric, Mr. Buhin testified in these proceedings, and he testified about that telephone call. And I'm referring to transcript 10016. And this is what he said. He said -- he was asked about the telephone call and said: "No, ours was a very short conversation. He" - referring to you - "only angrily told me not to butt in the work of the crime police, but to do my assigned job. That was the long and the short of our conversation." And then in his statement, P963, page 5 he says: "Eight or ten days after receiving that telephone call from Moric, I was returned to Zagreb. I was told the reason that I was withdrawn from Knin was that there was no need for two of us to be there. I do not remember the date that I left Knin. At any rate, my replacement arrived before I left. His name was Mato Markovic, and he was a traffic expert. He was there a few days before I left." So according to Mr. Buhin, you never informed him about his need to come back to Zagreb in the course of that telephone conversation. It was eight or ten days after your telephone conversation with Mr. Buhin that he was withdrawn, on the basis that there was no need for two people two police coordinators, in the field. So how do you reconcile your testimony that you just gave with what Mr. Buhin told this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, obviously, after such a long time, we don't remember the events in the same way, and that's the only possible explanation I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Now when you were questioned by the Bench about rotation, you said the rotation depended on the scope of the problems on the ground and the requirement of other types of experts. This is at page 35, line 6. And in fact during direct examination and cross-examination during last week, we saw a number of documents which showed that there was a problem of crimes continuing throughout the period until 15th September. Even at the Plitvice meeting, there was a discussion about meetings. Now, Mr. Buhin's area of responsibility was regular police. Wasn't that correct? As well as traffic regulation, regular police work and traffic regulation. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Madam Prosecutor, you are not right. The term regular police, in principle, covers all policing performed in uniform. However when it comes to the organisation and internal structure of the regular police, there is policing proper, traffic control, border control, airport control, and within that organisational structure, there is a clear definition about the jobs people perform within the sector of uniformed police. Mr. Buhin was in the ministry in the Department of Police, not in the sector of traffic police. He was, therefore, an expert for the general state of peace and order and prevention. He was not an expert in traffic; in other words, at that time, he did not deal in the matters within the purview of the traffic police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, Mr. Buhin testified in these proceedings, as I just told you. And this is at transcript page 9935. He testified that -- that he was responsible for the regular police work and traffic regulation. But be that as it may, my point is we saw records of situation where there are problems, serious crime being committed on the ground. So wouldn't you agree with me that this was a time at which you needed personnel of the Ministry of Interior whose expertise in fact were focused on regular police work, that is prevention of -- prevention of crime, and maintenance of law and order? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I agree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So then why withdraw Mr. Buhin whose expertise was in fact prevention of crime and maintenance of law and order and send down an expert in traffic matters? That doesn't -- almost sound consistent with what you have been saying all along in this Trial Chamber, which was that you were short of police resources. What is the logic behind that act?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a very clear logic, Madam Prosecutor. Last week, when I was examined by the Defence, we were faced with the facts that spoke about a very complicated -- the state of security in many other areas of our country at the time, not only in that area. And in the area where Operation Storm had taken place, we obviously needed traffic experts in the aftermath of Operation Storm. Mr. Buhin continued to perform his duties within the ministry, once he was withdrawn from Knin, and those duties covered the entire territory of the state. By doing that, he had just resumed where he had left off before being sent to the Knin area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, we saw your order dated 18th August, where you in fact even diverted resources as you said from crime investigation to crime prevention because the need was such. But here we have a situation, just a week after that, your order, you are sending a police coordinator whom you have initially sent down to the field to assist in the course of prevention of crime back to Zagreb. That somehow doesn't sound like a sincere effort towards prevention of crime. How do you respond to that?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Prosecutor, you are entitled to doubt the sincerity of the efforts, but we were involved in them on a daily basis. We needed men in other areas of the country that were also under -- that were under terrorist attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Just moving on, before I finish this topic, just one further question, Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I can have D360, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, while the document is coming up -- okay. We have -- You testified that documents addressed to the OA Povratak staff would reach you, or if you were not there you would be informed of the content in principle. Now this is a report sent to you by --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if could take the English document right to the top.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: By the Zadar-Knin police administration to you. It's dated 28th August. And it says: Subject, report on hygiene and sanitation measures pertaining to dead human bodies is being submitted. And it says that there is attached list. And if we could move to the next page, thank you, in the Croatian version also. Do you note, Mr. Moric, from number, 301 to 305 - that's five bodies - are the five civilians who were killed in Grubori? You have in fact received a report on the sanitation on the removal of those bodies. Now, at this stage when you received this report, didn't it occur to you to query as to why there -- you have not received a report on an on-site investigation into the matter, what had happened in this instance? Didn't it concern you to inquire into this matter, having received a report that five civilians were in fact killed in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Prosecutor, as before, when we discussed the conflict of professional opinions on this matter, you now again proceed from the basis that I or we in the police are duty-bound to be suspicious one of another. Such rules of mutual suspicion on the police force isn't something we have or something I have seen in the police systems worldwide. Therefore, when I received this report and, by the way, I'm not sure if I personally gave it any of my associates for consideration, but when I received it, it was confirmation to me that the system of the Ministry of the Interior had taken note of the incident and that, as the law dictates, all the mechanisms of the system would be activated and that everyone would do their part of the job.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, what is it -- what is contained in this report apart from the fact that these civilians bodies are buried in Knin cemetery to indicate to you that there has been an investigation, that the other, as to say, the system of the Ministry of Interior had taken note of the incident and the procedure, mechanisms have started working? What is in this document to indicate that to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Prosecutor, excuse me, but when you look at the document, it's quite clear. I am informed by the police administration of it, and it is the head of the police administration who signed it. Under the Law on The internal affairs, it is the police administration that is duty-bound to monitor the events, occurrences in its area, and report to the ministry. And I'm reported to by a person who has had his duties clearly defined by the law. Why should I be doubting that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Moric, I don't want to spend any further time on this subject. And moving on, I'd like you to look at your statement given to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if I could have, Mr. Registrar, D1842, the section marked 4893, page 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You discuss -- you discuss the inner control within the Ministry of Interior. And this is your testimony: "Inner control of the Ministry of the Interior dealt with discipline, disciplinary breaches, and work, whether the work was done according to the regulations for all members of the Ministry of Interior from the cleaning lady all the way to the minister, except in cases of special police. They had their own department of Control."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if we could move to page 18.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You say: "The way that inner control usually functions is they would receive information, tapes either from citizens or from the colleagues that somebody has done something, and then they would go and investigate [sic]."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And then if could you move to page 19.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You say: "Whenever I heard of dishonourable behaviour of anyone that falls under my responsibility, whether somebody immediately close or other, any police administration, I would not allow for anybody else but myself ... I would, myself, write to inner control to investigate the [sic] matter." Now just a matter which has not been properly clarified here. Now you say that the special police had their own inner control branch. So in the same way that the inner control of the Ministry of Interior worked, did the inner control of special police also conduct internal inquiries into the discipline and conduct of members of the special police?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Prosecutor, I think that the branch of the internal control of the special police had, as far as I remember, the role of gathering and processing information about discipline in the various units. However, the issue of disciplinary proceedings, just as was the case with the internal control at the level of the ministry overall, was not a matter for the internal control of the ministry overall and therefore, by the same token, either of the -- neither of the internal control of the special police. It was the chiefs of the police administrations who had to initiate them, and the disciplinary courts as independent judiciary bodies to hear them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, I did not about initiating disciplinary proceedings. My question was did the special police inner control branch work in the same manner as the inner control branch of the Ministry of Interior. I'm talking about -- I'm not asking about initiation of disciplinary proceedings. Was the task and the responsibility of the inner control of the special police the same vis-a-vis members of special police, police, as was the case with the inner control branch of the Ministry of Interior? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies, I now understand your question. Yes, my understanding of it is that they gathered information about the state of discipline in special police units.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, why is it -- why did the special police have their own inner control branch, as opposed to the rest of Ministry of Interior sectors having a different inner control?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two important reasons. One, of a practical nature. Unlike all the other employees of a police administration who were always moving over a certain area and were subject to public scrutiny, the special police role was quite different. They were supposed to provide security for various facilities in the face of violent behaviour, and I think that was one of the criteria. They were being singled out according to the areas where they were active, where they had to intervene and where they had to train. It was only logical for them to have their own mechanism of internal control, precisely for that reason. The second reason was that, as far as I know, the personnel, the human resources of the internal control of the special police, was used also to gather information relative to the areas where the special police was likely to operate. In semi-military or military jargon to make myself quite clear, when they -- their duty was to gather intelligence and counter-intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, if a member of a special police unit attached to a police administration commits a crime in the course of special police duties, and I would be specific, that would be while in the deployment of Operation Storm or in the course of any of the mop-up operations that were carried out after Operation Storm, who had the disciplinary authority to initiate disciplinary proceedings, that is, request for disciplinary proceedings against such member? Is it the special police sector command, or the chief of the police administration?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
