utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt my learned colleague. But the question was, in effect, ambiguous because my learned colleague in the first part of the question stated that, if a crime was committed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And in the other part [overlapping speakers]... about the disciplinary proceedings. So these are two different things, which are very much --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mikulicic, there are two different things. The one is to say the question is ambiguous, and then, of course, the first thing that comes to the mind of Ms. Mahindaratne and to my mind is that you should split up and not, as often happens, put into a question a lot of mixed information, and then, of course, to focus on one thing. The same -- Mr. Mikulicic, that's one thing. The other things is that we should not comment on the question because by saying what is wrong with the question, sometimes you give already a clue to the witness what apparently your concern may be. Therefore, Ms. Mahindaratne, could you please try to avoid questions in which the question in itself contains a lot of different matters and then, at the end, put a question to the witness where he could be confused by all the information you gave in the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So would you keep in mind what Mr. Mikulicic said and rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric the Trial Chamber has received evidence that in the case of a crime committed by a member of the special police, there are two processes, parallel processes, that take place. There is crime investigation by the crime police, and parallel to that disciplinary proceedings are initiated against him. That is, he is suspended and there is an internal disciplinary proceeding against him in the MUP disciplinary Courts. Now this Trial Chamber has heard that evidence. My question is, in such an event, where a member of the special police attached to a unit which is within a police administration - Your Honour, I'm referring to, let us say, a special police unit attached to Zagreb police administration - a member of such, is found to have committed a crime, and he is being investigated by the crime police, who would have the authority to suspend him and initiate disciplinary proceedings against him? Is it the special police sector command or the chief of the police administration to which the unit is attached?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Prosecutor, I have tried to understand your question. So a member of the special police has committed a crime, and for this reason, on the one hand, a criminal investigation has been launched, and, on the other he is suspended and disciplinary proceedings is initiated. Is my understanding of that situation correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct. And my question is who has the authority to initiate the disciplinary proceedings against him? Is it the special police sector command or the chief of the police administration, to which the special police unit is attached?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a special police expert. If you -- if you will allow me to, I'll answer the question the way I'm almost positive the procedure dictated. The commander of the unit of that particular member would, in cooperation with the internal control of the special police, gather all relevant information for disciplinary proceedings and forward the information to the person authorised with the power of initiating disciplinary proceedings, which is the chief of the police administration to which the special police unit belongs, or, as we call it in our police jargon, the parent police administration. So the head of that police administration had the power to initiate disciplinary proceedings before a disciplinary Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now didn't Mr. Markac have the power to initiate disciplinary proceedings against a member of a special police unit attached to a police administration if that conduct was -- if the conduct in question was committed in the course of Operation Storm or in the mop-up operations afterwards?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Markac, as well as all the others who belonged to the special police management, could, and was duty-bound, to forward the information he had of a breach of discipline or a crime to the person authorised to initiate disciplinary proceedings, which is the chief of the special -- of the police administration, to which the unit belongings.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, Mr. Cetina, the chief of police administration of Zadar-Knin police administration, testified here, as I told you, and when this question was asked of him, and this is at transcript reference 23593, let me just read this to you. This is what he said: "Now isn't it correct that if a member of the special police forces committed an offence that requests for disciplinary procedures, initiation of disciplinary had to be made by the commander of the special police and not yourself?" His response was: "Yes, that's how it was." According to Mr. Cetina, the authority to initiate disciplinary proceedings was with the commander of the special police sector and not himself. So are you -- is your testimony based on knowledge, or were you merely speculating when you said that it was the chief of the police administration?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Prosecutor, I am not speculating. I don't know why, and I'm even quite puzzled by what Mr. Cetina said. Perhaps because he was a chief of the police administration with least experience. But we can check the relevant documents, such as decisions rendered by disciplinary courts, and see that the authority was vested with chiefs of police administrations. They initiated disciplinary proceedings against all employees of their administration in the first instance.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Those documents are in evidence, Mr. Moric, so will not waste time calling them. But I want to show you a specific document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if could I have D530.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There was a discussion about who -- which sector within the Ministry of Interior could investigate crime. And I want to show you this document, Mr. Moric. And I appreciate you would not have seen this document. You wouldn't have had the opportunity. Or have you seen this document before? Let me just ask you that. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the additional notes, I can't conclude that it has ever reached me. I don't remember having seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, this, as you can see, is an order issued by Mr. Markac on 3rd October. And it's addressed to the special police unit commander of Zadar special police unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to object. This is not an order. Never in this document is written that type of text. So it could be not fair for the witness to present to him the piece of document which is defined as an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- this is a document issued by Mr. Markac on the 3rd of October, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are all aware that whether a document says order or not, if it says order, it is not necessarily order. Whether it also works the other way around is still to be established. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, here this document is sent to the chief of the Zadar-Knin police administration personally with the request that it be delivered to the special police unit commander. And Mr. Markac writes: "The special police sector received an Official Note from Gracac police station which states that on 17 September 1995 four members of the special police in a vehicle ... were noted in the village of Podkorina - I'm sorry I can't pronounce that - as they were leaving the site where a family home and a stable with hay were set on fire. "We checked and established that the above-mentioned vehicle is at the disposal of the SJP of the Zadar-Knin police administration." "In keeping with the above, you are to investigate" --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "In keeping with the above you are to investigate the above claims and submit in writing the results of the investigation to the special police sector." Now in issuing this order, from what you know, Mr. Moric, was Mr. Markac acting within his authority -- sorry, I rephrase, I'm sorry, in issuing this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry to be on my feet again, Your Honour, and my learned colleague. I think we have problem with -- I have -- I think we have problem of translation in that document. So the word in original "provjera," is basically wrongly translated. So if we could check what our translator in the courtroom could translate the word "provjera."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just ... The English -- is it the written translation that you have problems with?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Written translation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is -- yes, apparently what it -- the subject is described as "provjera informacije."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, and in the beginning of that part of the document it is translated like verification of information. And on the last paragraph of that document, the very same word, "provjera" is translated as investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The same word appears several times. Let me just check ... Now, Ms. Mahindaratne, are you willing to submit this document specifically for the purpose of the translation of the word "provjera"?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, it seems that the document tells the special police unit commander what to do and what -- and the results of this activity to be submitted to the special police sector. Do we agree on that, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's work on the basis of this wording and let's forget about the details which are still in dispute. Perhaps, Ms. Mahindaratne --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question, accordingly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, can you please look at this document and tell the Trial Chamber if, in issuing this document, was Mr. Markac acting within his authority?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, this document is in line with what we have spoken about, namely the procedure, when it comes to verifying and checking information to see if any of the special police has committed a breach of discipline, the way I understand it is that Mr. Markac received information based on which he concluded that that could have been the case and that it could have even been a potential crime and the breach of discipline and that's why he wanted the information verified and checked and the verification result to be submitted to him. I assume that he would then follow the logic of conveying information further onto the person who would be responsible for starting criminal proceedings. In other words, this document was issued by Mr. Markac and sent with the purpose of verifying information.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you have given a lengthy answer to that, Mr. Moric, but you haven't told me what I asked you. Was Mr. Markac acting within his authority when this document was issued? That was my question. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, I believe that he was acting within his authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I could have, Mr. Registrar, D531, please. And we will see, Mr. Moric, a document on the screen by which the special police commander of Zadar has responded to this instruction by Mr. Markac, the very next day. And that's -- he says, report. And he reports that: "Pursuant to request for information verification ... the information was checked out, and it was positively determined that the perpetrator of the arson in the village of Podkorina ... was an officer of the Zadar-Knin police administration special police unit." Now -- and then there is further details about that crime. Now, the Trial Chamber has received evidence that the special police was a highly-skilled elite police force. Apart from the combat operations they carried out, did they also have the ability to investigate crime, if necessary?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, you mean in the same way it would have been done by the authorised and professional crime police? In the same way? You mean that the -- whether the special police could have done the same as the crime police?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No. Whether the special police had the capacity to verify, let us say, as to whether in fact indeed a member of the unit has committed a crime. In the manner that has been done in this report, to your knowledge, did they have the competence to do that? Not legally, but could they do -- carry it out, if necessary?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, does your question refer specifically to the event described in this report?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, we can see in this report that the event was a case of some cattle food being set on fire. And that fact could be established, it's something that could you see, that you can simply state, that some dry grass burned down. However, when it comes down to crime investigation, I don't think that the special police was either trained or equipped to do that, nor was it its task.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, let me move onto another area. And in fact Mr. Kay went through a series of documents with you on the planning of the operation. Isn't it correct that prior to the commencement of Operation Storm you and your colleagues at the Ministry of Interior had the experience of crimes being committed in the liberated territories after the previous operations; for example, in operation -- after Operation Medak and Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had experience, or, rather, experiences that taught us that there were different problems and that we were able to face all sorts of crimes that we were -- potentially or looking at facing all sorts of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, those crimes that were committed in Operation Medak and Flash, to your knowledge, were they investigated?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I believe that this is a generally known fact. People have been sentenced for crimes committed in the territory of Medak, and they're still serving those sentences.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, I'd like you to look at what you told the Office of the Prosecutor, which is in evidence, your statement, D1842, and if could you turn to the second section. Not the one that you're looking, Mr. Moric, at now. The second section, the middle one. That's section 4893, page 53.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, did I understand you well that the previous document about the investigation of the haystack put on fire of -- or -- you just focus on the investigation. You did not want to pay any further attention to the measures taken as a result? Which is fine, but I just want to know whether you want to limit what you put to this witness to the investigations, rather than to the measures that were taken, such as the removed from duty and cut in salary, that's not something you --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I didn't need to go into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If could you focus on page 53, Mr. Moric. Now, you were in fact asked whether you knew about -- this is the question: "You mentioned that you were aware of some problems. Were you aware of any, let us say, military personnel, having been prosecuted for any crimes during that period?" This is with regard to the previous operations. The question you just answered. This is your response: "I do not know if anybody was processed for the crimes [sic]. What I know that there were problems and that they were reported. Whether or not they were investigated by the investigative judge and ... whether or not these investigations resulted in indictments ... or if somebody was charged with any of these [sic] crimes, I do not know. I do not know that." Now you just told in Court the exact opposite. How do you reconcile your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Does this refer to the document you're showing me? And does that all that refer to the territory of Medak?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, I asked you if you were aware that the crimes committed in the previous operations were investigated, and you answered, this was your answer: "Madam Prosecutor I believe that this is a generally known fact. People have been sentenced for crimes committed in the territory of Medak, and they're still serving those sentences." Now you were asked about questions -- about crimes committed in the previous -- let me first ask you one further question. Do you know if the crimes committed in Operation Flash, whether they were investigated?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crime investigation after that, an investigation, you know, that was not my job. At that time, it was not part of my duties no know whether such investigations were carried out or not. That's why I asked you just a minute ago with the way I spoke to Mr. Foster, with regard to Medak Pocket, I answered Mr. Foster's questions, and I told him what I knew at the time, when things were actually happening. The perspective is different, and hence, the difference in the answers I provided to Mr. Foster, as opposed to the answers I'm providing to you today.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let's move away from perspective, Mr. Moric. Let me ask you a clear question. Are you aware if the crimes committed in Operation Medak and Operation Flash were investigated? Do you know, to your knowledge, if they were investigated or not? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the media, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you were -- you were -- you were the assistant minister of interior. Wouldn't you know if crimes were investigated or not, because if there was an investigation, fundamental police would be involved in the -- the on-site investigations. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, at the level of the Ministry of the Interior, we followed trends. We did not analyse any concrete and specific cases. That would have been contrary to the law. We never dwelled upon the concrete proceedings in certain cases. There were teams of experts in charge of dealing with every single concrete case. That was their job.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I understand your testimony, Mr. Moric, in your position as assistant minister of interior, because you followed trends, you would not know -- you would not be in a position to say if crimes were investigated or not. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I hate to interrupt. Are we talking about Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We're talking about Operation Medak and Operation Flash.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I refer my learned friend to page 51 of 4893, line 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, for the later transcript I usually have the pages attached to it. Could you give me a date, then so that I'm at least in the right transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. It is on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, you said 489...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 165 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's exhibit 1842 which is on -- D1842 which is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I have found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I -- yes, I should I -- I was thinking in terms of transcript pages, rather than -- I do understand you said page 51 of -- yes, now I just misunderstood. It was my mistake. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Moric, this is what you have said in relation to crimes committed in Operation Flash, and this is at page 51 of your transcript, if you turn to the previous page. You say: "Were you aware in your position as assistant minister and your subsequent negotiations of any crimes being committed by Croatian military?" You say: "Where?" And this is page 51. "In Sector West. That's during and after Operation Flash itself. Yes, I heard about, I heard that there were problems. I heard that there were some suspicious deaths, and I know that crime police investigated it. An investigation of those crimes would be -- the detail of these investigations would kept where?" And there is a discussion about that. And at page 53, Mr. Moric, you are asked again: "You mentioned that you were aware of some problems. Were you aware of any, let us say, military personnel having been prosecuted for any crimes during that period?" Your responses is: "I do not know if anybody was processed for the crime. What I know ... there were problems and that they were reported. Whether or not they were investigated by the investigative judge and ... whether or not these investigations resulted in indictments ... if somebody was charged with any of these [sic] crimes, I do not know. I do not know that." Now, the question was asked from you as to -- as to -- as assistant minister of the interior if you are aware as to whether crimes committed by military personnel during Operation Flash were processed and whether anyone was charged. You have said that you were aware that crime police investigated it, but are you not aware as to if anyone was charged or not. Now, how is it, Mr. Moric, that you're holding a very senior position in the Ministry of Interior that you're not able to say if anyone was charged for crimes committed in Operation Flash or not? You were the assistant minister of uniformed police at the time.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, it is correct that I was the assistant minister in charge of uniformed police and prevention. I was not in charge of crime police and crime investigation, detecting crimes. In principle, everybody did their own job. I managed the work of the uniformed police, and I had a colleague who was in charge of managing the work of the crime police. Of course, in day-to-day operations, we meet on a daily basis and exchange information in order to be able to monitor trends. And I knew, based on that information, that there had been some suspicious deaths and that the crime police would get involved and try to elucidate those suspicious deaths. It is only logical that, at the time, when Mr. Foster and I spoke, I didn't know whether that would result in any indictments or charges being brought against certain individuals and their sentencing. In addition to that, Madam Prosecutor, I was a member of the executive power, and tripartite division of power is very well known. Judiciary is independent, and they don't have to inform us as to what they do. That's why I told you that from public sources of information I learned that people had been sentenced for crimes committed in the territory of Medak.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, you were interviewed by Mr. Foster in 2004. So if anyone was to be charged for crimes committed in Operation Flash which was May 1995, by that time, if you were going to get such information, you would have known that, wouldn't it? I say that because you said by the time -- at the time I spoke with Mr. Foster, you didn't know if people were going to be indicted or not.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Prosecutor, I said something that was even more precise than that. At the time of my discussions with Mr. Foster concerning the time-period we discussed, and that was the period of Operation Flash, we spoke of 1995, and, unfortunately, this is the period under discussion today as well. However, the crime police was not duty-bound in specific matters to inform the assistant minister in charge of the uniformed police of their activities. In fact the key report on the work of the crime police can be found in the criminal reports that the -- the crime police files through -- to -- to the competent prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So based on what you just said, Mr. Moric, then it would be correct to assume - and you can correct me if I'm wrong - that you would not be a position to say as to if people -- if anybody was charged for crimes committed in Operation Storm either. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke of Operation Flash a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying. Based on what you said, you said that the crime police was not bound to inform you. You didn't get this information because you were in charge of uniformed police, and as such you are not in a position to say as to -- if people had been investigated and if people had been charged after Operation Flash. If that's the case, the same principle would apply in relation to Operation Storm. Isn't that right, Mr. Moric? You would not be in a position then to tell this Trial Chamber if persons were indeed properly investigated and charged in relation to crimes committed in Operation Storm. Because the same level of information that you received in relation to Operation Flash would apply here, in relation to Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, Mrs. Prosecutor. This follows from the way in which the Ministry of the Interior was organised and the way in which it worked, as provided for by the relevant decree.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm told that it is time for a break. This would be a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know who told you. But it is certainly approximately -- I would, however, deal with two minor procedural matters, but we don't need Mr. Moric for that. Mr. Moric, if you could already follow -- we would like to see you -- the usher, then we would like to see you back in 20 to 25 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, first of all, thank you for sending your e-mail which certainly is helpful for the Chamber. When we invited you, we also invited the Prosecution to tell us about any developed plans for calling rebuttal evidence. Mr. Waespi could you inform the Chamber about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes. We have no plans to call any rebuttal witnesses at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this point in time. Thank you for that. Then there was a translation issue in relation to P27 -- 2678. I think you raised it, Mr. Misetic. It was Mr. Carrier who introduced the document, and I think the Prosecution was invited to check the translation of that document. Any report on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just report as soon after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may do so. Then, finally, there is a request pending for adding two witnesses to your 65 ter list. One of them being Witness MM-026, which is the witness scheduled first in the first week of January, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That is correct Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now the Chamber was about to finalize a decision on the matter, but a filing of last Friday, because the two witnesses you are seeking leave to be added to your 65 ter list, your filing of last Friday doesn't deal in any way with Witness MM-026, as you have called her, however, the Chamber is not in a position at this moment to deliver its written decision on the matter, because the filing of last Friday complicates at least the other part, that is MM-027. Now we thought that it was urgent for you to know whether we would at least grant the request in relation to Witness MM-026 because she was scheduled for later in December. Now she has been moved to early January. At the same time, you announce that perhaps one of the witnesses in the week of the 14th to the 18th of December might not be available. So not knowing whether you would like to fill that gap with Witness MM-026, the Chamber considers it wise already to inform you about the decision, that leave is granted to add Witness MM-026 to your 65 ter list. I've got no idea whether there are any request for protective measures, that's the reason I'm using -- not. Then we are talking about Snjezana Bagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I'm afraid that witness -- the number MM-026 has already been assigned earlier to another witness, so I would -- I would invite you to -- to assign another number to Snjezana Bagic, and where I earlier said that leave is granted to add Witness MM-026, I'm now more precise and saying that leave is granted to add Snjezana Bagic to your 65 ter list, although another MM number --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It will be MM-028 Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Twenty-eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And just to inform you, as we put Ms. Bagic to testify on the first week of January, in our schedule it was done with exchange of consultation with my learned colleague Mr. Waespi, and that's for -- that's we moved her on the beginning of the next year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that that has got something do with availability of expert knowledge in the Prosecution team on the matter Witness Bagic will testify about?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is correct, Mr. President. And in addition to what's being said right now, I would like to inform that you we would like to respond or to reply to the response by the Markac Defence on the second expert. I forgot the number. I think it is Witness 27 to be added. I believe we have 14 days or something, but we will certainly respond by Wednesday or Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has received this filing, and the Chamber will consider how to proceed with that, but does not obstruct you at this moment from preparing a further submission. Although there is no commitment by the Chamber at this moment that this is the by receiving further submissions that that's how we want to deal with the matter. It's fresh. It arrived, I think, two minutes to 4.00 on Friday. We have looked at it over the weekend and this morning. We will further consider that matter as soon as possible. These were the procedural matters I had on my list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just to stress the point that the leave from my learned colleague to reply would be in fact surreply to response to reply. So just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But at least Mr. Waespi indicates that everything will be done within the time-limits that's already -- in this context --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That will be helpful of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that's something new at all. We will -- it was clear, Mr. Mikulicic, where we are with this -- with this witness who is an expert witness. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at 1.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I took a risk by saying sharp. This is not to -- to be interpreted that "sharp" is ten minutes after the time indicated. The Chamber apologises, but we had urgent matters to deal with, which took more time than expected. Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. Mr. Registrar, may I have D409, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, I'm going to call up some documents that we have already looked at. And this is in relation to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, if you could go to the Croatian page 4, and the English page 5, I would be grateful, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We already looked at this document, Mr. Moric. This is the meeting on 2nd August, where you met with the -- with your minister, Mr. Jarnjak, and the minister of defence, Mr. Susak. Now can you tell the Trial Chamber at these meetings, was there a discussion about crimes committed in the previous operations, particularly in Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, but may I, before answering your question, see the list of attendees?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm referring to the meeting at 7.30 where the minister -- it's right in front of your screen, Mr. Moric --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, it's 1730.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 1730. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You misspoke. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm referring to the meeting at 1730 where the minister of defence, the minister of interior, and yourself, you met, which is right in front of your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We see it in English, but Mr. Moric could not yet see it in the B/C/S version. He now can. You see it at the bottom of the page, Mr. Moric? Yes? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was it just the three of you who met, or were there other people at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I see the rest of the document? To see if there was anyone else present.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We could go do the next page. But don't you recall that meeting? You already spoke about it during Mr. Kay's examination.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's just that I would like to see precisely what the document states. You asked me if there were other persons in attendance at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, I only asked that in response to when you raised it. My question was really was in relation to this meeting: Were crimes committed in previous operations, specifically in Operation Flash, discussed at this meeting, between Minister Jarnjak, Minister Susak, and yourself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. I just -- I rise with this particular document being shown to the witness, and we had some questions go back and forth. But if the witness can be informed what this document is that is he being -- that he is looking at. I can advise the Court what it is, but I'm sure counsel knows what it is as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Mahindaratne, you refer to the fact that the witness, that questions were put in relation to the witness. But if in half a line you could say this the meeting, then the day, 2nd of August, because that seems to be the date --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But it goes to the question of the number of attendees and this came in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne understands that she is briefly in half a line, to introduce the meeting to the witness so that he is better able to orient himself. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, we in fact discussed this during Mr. Kay's examination with you. You recall there was a meeting on 2nd August between Mr. Susak, the defence minister, Mr. Jarnjak, minister of the interior, and yourself, which took place at 1730. This document is the minutes of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. That is not the minutes of the meeting. These are -- General Lausic's notes of that meeting to which he attended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. My apologies. I should have specifically said. I actually forgot, Mr. President, that was the reason. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is not official minutes, Mr. Moric, I should have mentioned that. This is General Lausic extract of his diary. Now, do you -- you recall this meeting. You didn't have a problem about this when, in fact, when Mr. Kay examined you on this document.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the meeting but, excuse me, I was puzzled by the mention of the minutes, because I don't recall the minutes, and that's why I asked to see who was present in order to be able to think back within that context.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My apologies, my mistake. Now you now exactly what this document is. Now, I'm going to the meeting. My question to you is, at this meeting -- and we don't have to focus on this document for it. At this meeting, were crimes committed in the previous operations, Operation Medak, and specifically Operation Flash, discussed between Mr. Susak, Mr. Jarnjak, and yourself? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Once again, if I could just put it this in context, Mr. President. General Lausic is there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think this should be discussed in the presence of the witness if Mr. Kehoe is going to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think that the document should be accurately presented to the witness that these are notes taken by General Lausic at this meeting. And if that's what this -- has been discussed throughout this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Mahindaratne, do you agree that these are the notes taken by Mr. Lausic?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then why not --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I said that to the witness. I don't know why Mr. Kehoe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see what exactly you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can look page 70, line 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm -- as a matter of fact, we should stop these kind of discussions. These are the notes made by Mr. Lausic on that meeting. Please put your question, preferably a question without too many further introductions. I think -- The question was whether you remember, that at this meeting, crimes committed during Operation Flash were discussed, yes or no. Could you tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I recall that we discussed the matter as a problem that we were faced with, and that should not be repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Place your next question, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: At that meeting, was it discussed that the crimes were committed in -- that the crimes that were committed in Operation Flash were committed by military personnel? Was that fact discussed?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We discussed about -- the problem as a problem that existed, regardless of who committed it. Unfortunately, there were crimes committed by both civilians and soldiers, or individuals in uniforms. Our discussions were of a general nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, is it correct that this meeting was conducted for purposes of planning the policing of the liberated territory; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Prosecutor, unfortunately, that's not true. The ministers of defence and internal affairs are not the ones that are competent for this sort of planning. This was a general meeting, at which the ministers cautioned about the problem that we had earlier on, and the fact that Mr. Lausic and I were supposed to be in charge of the whole matter at the operative level in such a way as to prevent such crimes committed and, if that should prove possible, to reduce them to the minimum.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, your testimony is that at this meeting, you said we discussed about the problem as a problem that existed regardless of who committed it. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what exactly was discussed in terms of the crimes at this meeting, without just saying to generally discuss, can you tell the Trial Chamber what was the -- the line of the conversation? Was it stated that crimes could be committed again after Operation Storm because the same thing had happened in Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Prosecutor, at the ministerial level, this was roughly how matters stood. The ministers would refer to a problem and present a position on it. They do not go into analysing or planning operative procedures --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, if I could interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But if you insist I could --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you as to how the ministers generally do it -- speak. But my question is, you were present at this meeting. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what exactly was stated with regard to crimes committed in previous operations. Was it said that the same thing could happen after Operation Storm? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was said that we might have these problems all over again and that we should get organised in such a way as to make sure that they do not occur or that they occur as few and far between and possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, if the witness has told us that they discussed that they should not be repeated, would that not automatically include that you considered the possibility that it would happen again? Otherwise, there's no need, is there, to discuss that it should not happen again. So, therefore, that is part of the answer which -- I do not understand what then the -- what you're seeking to establish.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I will just go to the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, was it discussed at this meeting that in Operation Flash, there was a problem about the military police cooperating with the Ministry of Interior forces in addressing crimes committed by military personnel? Was that discussed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I cannot confirm this with any certainty. I do not rule out the possibility that this was discussed too. It's just that I can't be certain that this was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Looking at Mr. Lausic's notes here, if you could focus on what the minister of the interior, Mr. Jarnjak, had stated. He writes: "It cannot be the same model as Operation Flash as more places will be occupied. The military police follow the front line and the civilian police enter populated areas." And the third point is: "Shutting down of catering establishments within a 50-kilometre range from a place ordered by government." Is that a reference to shutting down establishments where alcohol was being served? Is that a reference from your recollection; could you say?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly, I don't recall the topic as noted down by Mr. Lausic, as having been discussed at the meeting. However, based on the formulation here and based on my police experience, I can state that this referred to catering establishments because that was where large groups of people normally gather and they might be at risk of artillery fire or multi-barrel rocket-launcher fire from occupied areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The fourth point is: "Introduction of curfew." And it says, "Karlovac, Sisak, Gospic, Zadar, Sibenik." Now after Operation Storm, the initial attack was completed, was a curfew imposed?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was it that every contemplated, Mr. Moric, for instance when the Ministry of Interior faced problems in controlling the crimes? Was that ever contemplated, Mr. Moric, when, for instance, the Ministry of Interior faced problems in controlling the crimes? Was it ever contemplated, perhaps a curfew, imposing a curfew might help the Ministry of Interior to bring the territory under control?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My associates and lower level teams of specialists contemplated this idea, but, in this particular problem, as was the case with others, too, there was a discrepancy between the peacetime mechanism of activity and wartime circumstances, and one always had to find this fine line in the restriction of movement of citizens at large.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Moric, we heard on a number of occasions you said -- told the Trial Chamber how it was difficult to control the situation. Now, understandably, this is wartime. But what was the difficulty in imposing a curfew to enable the law enforcement forces to address the situation more fully or better? What was the problem that you had?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem was in the concept of a democratic and civic state. In an area that was occupied a day or two previously, should the same or similar state of affairs be introduced, and, thus, shutting it out of any normal activity. The idea was to normalize the situation. In practical terms, had we, over such a vast territory, introduced or imposed a curfew, we would have difficulties in implementing this measure alone. Last week, we mentioned the 11.000 square kilometres, numerous local and dirt roads. With a curfew imposed, the job would have been practically impossible to carry out, if the police had to patrol the area for persons who were in breach of curfew and concentrate on these matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me call --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have D45, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you will see in a moment, Mr. Moric, that will be official minutes of your working meeting with the military police administration officials on 3rd August.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if you could go to -- in English page 4, Mr. Registrar, and Croatian page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There, in the English page, the last page, and in the Croatian, if could you move to the next page, please. This refers to a statement you made at that meeting, Mr. Moric. This is what you say: "He further said that ... in Western Slavonia he had noticed activities of loose cannons, persons who did not take part in combat activities but were spotted in the area of the front line wearing HV uniforms, raiding houses and 'administering rough justice.' He also pointed out that occurrences of abuse of MUP uniforms had been noticed, namely four persons were found. They are in MUP uniforms. And only later it turned out that they were SIS employees." Now, earlier on, you told the Trial Chamber that you had no information of the investigations or charges processed against crimes committed in Operation Flash. So if you didn't have that information, how were you then able to describe the categories of perpetrators and to say that some were wearing HV uniforms and some were not taking part in combat activities, they were loose cannons, I mean how were you able to give this type of description if in fact you had no information on the investigations conducted into those crimes?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I didn't say that I didn't have any information at all. I told you that we were well-informed about trends and that we monitored trends. It is true that I was never informed about any investigations in any particular cases, because that was not a subject of my interest and that was also not my responsibility. In other words, I was only informed about trends. And here we're talking about loose cannons, and that was one of the trends recorded at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could move to the next page in the English document. And the Croatian, we can remain on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There's report on what Major-General Lausic had said. He said: "He said in his introductory address that the meeting of ministers which had been held the previous day as well as a meeting of the highest officials an officers of the HV held in the war room of the Ministry of Defence had, among others, rendered the military police and the MUP responsible for complete efficiency in carrying out tasks during combat activities of the HVO. He also pointed out that the commanders of the HV units were warned that they would be personally responsible for the discipline of their subordinates. Otherwise, not even a much larger number of the military police force would be able to secure discipline?" Do you recall General Lausic making that statement at this meeting? This is the working meeting on 3rd August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I think if we look at the -- I apologise. If we look at the Croatian, I believe that line should be HV and not HVO, if we look at the original, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. Thanks, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you then invite the witness to -- to answer the question but then the right version which is in his own language.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You could read, Mr. Moric, General Lausic's statement there in Croatian and tell me if you recall that statement being made at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Madam Prosecutor. In this document, Mr. Lausic mentions two meetings from the day before. He says that there were two meetings the day before. The first one was a meeting of the ministers of defence and the interior, and then, a meeting of the top officials and officers of the Croatian Army. As far as I can remember, the second meeting of the top officials and officers of the Croatian Army which could include what is mentioned in here is the meeting that I didn't attend, and I wouldn't know whether Mr. Lausic spoke about that or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You misunderstood, Mr. Moric. My question was: At this meeting, this minute says that General Lausic said at the third meeting that, At the previous meeting such and such was discussed. I'm not asking about whether General Lausic said anything of this sort at the previous meeting. My question is at the working meeting on 3rd with the minister of the interior officers, including your yourself, do you recall General Lausic making a statement that at the previous meeting, this statement had been made. That is my question.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise for having misunderstood you the first time around. I don't remember him saying that. However, I don't have any reason to doubt the document which says that he did say that. I can only believe that he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if we could just move, Mr. Registrar, to page 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There, page 7 of the English, and in the Croatian it's page 4. There you are -- Major Lausic saying this: "He informed those present about the order issued by the Minister of Defence according to which the only persons allowed to enter the area of combat activities would be those having a permission signed by the assistant minister, Brigadier Markica Rebic, and by the chief of the political administration, Major-General Ivan Tolj." And then he goes on to say: "With regard to the meetings, he informed those present about the order according to which every visit by foreign citizens would be registered in the form about which the SIS would be informed." You go on to say: "The Assistant Minister Josko Moric announced that entries and exits of towns were going to be secured, as part of the MUP preparations." Now, those passes that General Lausic refers to, for how long did those -- did they operate or were they valid after the liberation of the territory?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, this document says that they were applicable to the area where there was combat going on. So it is only logical that they were valid for as long as combat was going on, and as soon as the combat was over, there was no need to have them in place.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you say it's logical, to your knowledge, do you know a particular point at which these passes were not required for people to enter the combat territory? What is your knowledge, Mr. Moric, on this issue? I'm not asking you to tell what's logical.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I really don't remember that we ever had any problem with this. This was public knowledge. I don't know for how long the passes were valid or that we had any problem with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, according to what you said at this meeting, the fundamental police were to secure the entries and exits of towns. Was that done? Did you implement that order -- did you implement that plan?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We could see that from some of the documents presented last week work orders issued to commanders and police officers, and their reports speaking about checks that they performed at the exits and entrances into the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in addition to that, isn't it correct that you also issued an order to close down the roads to civilian traffic, as of 3.00 a.m. on 4th August? And if you want to, I can also show you your order.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do that, Ms. Mahindaratne, I'm looking at the clock. It is quarter to 2. If we start now discussing a new document, and I take it that you have a few questions for the witness on that, then I'd rather first now adjourn so that we can continue tomorrow. Could I ask you, are you on schedule? You said you expected less than the six.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I wouldn't go -- I certainly won't go beyond six, but I expected only about five, perhaps going a little over. At this stage, it's difficult for me to say if I would go to the sixth session, but certainly five session, which would mean by the second session tomorrow, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you could try to elicit the evidence as focused as possible, that would save time. Mr. Moric, you receive the same instructions that you received before, that is, that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, testimony already given today or last week, or testimony still to be given. And we'd like to see you back tomorrow at 9.00, because we adjourn, and we will resume, Tuesday, the 8th of December, at 9.00 in Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 8th day of December, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
